editions.title: Tech shares slump as US midterms revive AI slowdown fears
editions.notification: Nasdaq's worst day in 18 months as Democrats' midterm win sparks data centre curbs fears. Here's what's next.
editions.intro:
Global tech shares suffered their sharpest sell-off in well over a year after Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Investors expect tighter scrutiny of AI data centres, with Democrats having promised a national moratorium on new facilities. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 per cent on Thursday, its worst day in 18 months, and entered correction territory, wiping out an estimated $2tn to $2.5tn. Nvidia fell 9.2 per cent, and chipmakers including AMD, Micron and Infineon were hit hard across markets.

The contagion spread quickly. Japan's Nikkei dropped below 60,000 points for the first time since May, falling 6.3 per cent at one point, while South Korea's Kospi triggered a circuit breaker after falling more than 8 per cent. Taiwan had its worst week since 2001. The sell-off has also reached credit markets, with SoftBank leading losses in Asian dollar bonds, and Indian equities were among the few gainers in the region. The FTSE 100 was little changed, closing down 0.4 per cent.

The political backdrop is now central to the industry's outlook. Elon Musk spent around $450m backing Republicans and still saw losses, including in Texas, and his companies Tesla and SpaceX fell. OpenAI and Amazon have responded with pledges to drop NDAs with officials and to cover power costs for data centre projects. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has blamed opponents for the fall, so the policy direction for AI infrastructure will be a key thing to watch.

top_stories.title: Global tech stocks plunge as midterms revive AI slowdown fears
top_stories.summary: Tech shares fell across the US, Europe and Asia after Democrats took both houses of Congress, with campaigns focused on slowing data centre growth. Around $2.5tn was wiped from the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent. Democrats have promised a national data centre moratorium, which investors are pricing in.

top_stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to drop NDAs with public officials, pay the full cost of its electricity and infrastructure, and publish local job forecasts. The move follows voter opposition to data centre expansion and mirrors an Amazon pledge.

editions.title: Midterm shockwaves hit AI and chip stocks; China reportedly blocks SoftBank-ABB deal
editions.notification: Democrats' midterm sweep rattles AI and chip stocks, and China reportedly blocks SoftBank's ABB robotics bid.
editions.intro:
The Democratic sweep of the US midterms dominated the day's tech news. Asian chip stocks slid, with South Korea's Kospi falling as much as 4.67% before a trading halt, and Samsung and SK hynix under pressure. Investors fear a Democrat-led Congress could tighten rules on AI data centres and scrutinise Trump-era AI and crypto trades. US markets recovered on Tuesday, with Nvidia up 2.3%, after the Nasdaq had briefly entered correction territory. Data centres were a clear election issue: an NBC exit poll found almost 80% of respondents opposed them in their neighbourhoods, and local measures restricting construction passed almost everywhere. Musk's record spending of around $450m for Republicans largely failed, and his companies now face likely tougher scrutiny.

Corporate news was mixed. AMD posted a record quarter, with revenue of $13.4bn and data centre making up about 63% of sales, and forecast $17bn next quarter, though its gaming business fell 40%. Apple shares dropped after it warned of thinner margins from higher memory costs. Uber reported strong third-quarter bookings of $59.8bn, but Waymo pulled out of its app in Austin and Atlanta the same day. In Europe and Asia, China reportedly blocked SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics unit, an FT report that is not yet confirmed.

Elsewhere, Google will switch off its AI features by default for K-12 student accounts, a move that drew criticism from New York's mayor. Cyber-attacks on European cold storage, including France's blood service, continued, with no group claiming responsibility. Anthropic and OpenAI both announced product and policy updates, including new image watermarking for older Claude models and animated GIF generation in ChatGPT.

top_stories.summary: Exit polls showed strong opposition to data centres, and local measures restricting them passed in several states. Construction moratoriums and grid-cost rules are likely next, with Goldman Sachs flagging possible delays in Georgia and Texas.

top_stories.title: Local data centre measures largely voted down across the US
top_stories.summary: Of about 40 local measures, only one favoured expansion. Six outright bans passed, and two mayors were recalled over data centre disputes, signalling more scrutiny ahead.

top_stories.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose on Tuesday after a brief slide that pushed the Nasdaq into correction. Nvidia gained 2.3% while Apple fell 1.9% on a weaker margin forecast.

top_stories.title: AMD posts record quarter on data centre demand
top_stories.summary: AMD reported record revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre at about 63% of sales. It forecasts $17bn next quarter and over 80% growth in 2027, though gaming revenue fell 40%.

top_stories.summary: The FT reports China's state planner opposed SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics arm. The report is unconfirmed, and SoftBank is weighing whether to seek approval again.

editions.title: Fridge hacks spread across Europe as AMD posts record quarter
editions.notification: Supermarket fridges hacked across Europe, while AMD reports its best quarter ever.
editions.intro:
A suspected cyber-attack is spreading across Europe. Supermarket chains in at least seven countries, including Ahold Delhaize, Ikea, Carrefour Belgium and Colruyt, reported freezer temperatures rising overnight to as high as 50C, and some stores pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, and experts warned that many refrigeration controllers are reachable online and unpatched. It follows a French attack last month that affected hundreds of supermarkets. The UK's AI minister said a serious cyber breach is "extremely likely", and the NCSC warned that British firms were wilfully blind to threats.

In markets, the story was chipmakers. AMD reported a record $13.4 billion quarter, with data centre revenue of $8.5 billion, and guided to about $17 billion next quarter, while Intel guided to $15-16 billion. Its shares rose about 5% after hours, and analysts see AMD possibly overtaking Intel as the largest x86 chip vendor. AMD's gaming revenue fell 40%, however, as memory shortages driven by AI demand squeeze consumer hardware. Apple also reported a record iPhone quarter of $57.58 billion, up 17%, despite no standard iPhone launch, though it warned of higher memory costs.

Political and market backdrop was volatile. Democrats swept key US midterm races, including Texas, and European and Asian tech shares fell on expectations of tougher scrutiny of Trump-era policies. US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after the Nasdaq had entered correction territory on Monday. Oracle reportedly dropped a $7 billion Tencent AI deal under US pressure, a single-source report that is worth watching.

editions.title: Apple beats on iPhone as Anthropic's compute bill tops $1trn
editions.notification: Apple's iPhone sales hit a record without a standard iPhone. Anthropic's compute commitments near $1trn. Read the briefing.
editions.intro:
Apple dominated the day's financial news. Its fourth-quarter results showed iPhone revenue of $57.58bn, up 17% year on year, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and by price rises on older models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn, services reached $31.57bn and the Mac grew 24%, while iPad fell 10%. Chief executive John Ternus said memory costs were rising but partly offset. The foldable iPhone Duo, priced at $1,999, sold out quickly, and Apple said supply will be hard to predict. Apple's results are reported in the quarter to September, and its first full report under Ternus is due on 2 November.

The AI sector drew attention too. Anthropic's revised IPO filing shows roughly $895bn of compute and infrastructure commitments, which could top $1trn with other obligations. Revenue for the nine months to September reached $33.2bn, but the company warns that such rapid growth is unlikely to continue, and only about $213bn of the commitments can be avoided. Separately, the Financial Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia has told cloud partners to reduce exposure to Chinese clients, a move Nvidia has not confirmed. Palantir also reported a strong quarter, with US commercial revenue overtaking US government revenue for the first time, though its shares fell 3.1% before volatile after-hours trading.

Elsewhere, SpaceX is reportedly eyeing a purchase of Boost Mobile from EchoStar to gain tower access for Starlink phone service, though carriers have reportedly rejected earlier approaches. Across Europe, supermarket fridges and freezers were hit by a suspected cyber-attack spreading to at least seven countries, and Meta delayed new business terms after pushback over web scraping. Samsung retained the top smartphone spot in the third quarter as the overall market shrank 20%.

top_stories.title: Apple posts record iPhone quarter without a standard iPhone
top_stories.summary: Apple's quarterly iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58bn, driven by the iPhone 18 Pro range and price rises on older models. Total revenue reached $114.5bn, with services at $31.57bn. Ternus said memory costs were partly offset by inventory and lower component costs.

editions.title: Chip crunch deepens as Altman meets Samsung; Binance outflows
editions.notification: Memory chip shortage deepens as Sam Altman meets Samsung, and Binance users pull $3.6bn after its heist.
editions.intro:
The memory chip shortage dominated the last 24 hours. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman met roughly 50 Samsung executives at the company's Yongin site on Saturday, with Samsung confirming the talks covered how AI could reshape industries and business. No supply deals were announced, though memory supply is widely assumed to have been on the agenda. The meeting fits a wider pattern: Samsung and SK hynix are signing long-term customer agreements years ahead, with SK hynix saying its DRAM and HBM output is effectively sold out through 2029, yet both shares remain well below their 52-week highs.

Crypto was the other major theme. Binance users withdrew about $3.6bn as the exchange restarted services after a heist. The FBI and TRM Labs attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, and Binance says it has found further breach points. Binance has pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen. Separately, French lawmakers voted narrowly to add a traffic-based levy on content providers to the 2027 budget. The amendment still has to clear further budget stages, and the government opposed it.

Elsewhere, Intel and AMD may be exploring cooperation, though neither has confirmed details. Spotify is reportedly preparing an AI product with a possible premium surcharge, and Apple's first results under CEO John Ternus are due on 2 November. Most other items are rumours or product news with limited near-term market impact.

editions.title: Amazon's AI spend, Microsoft buyouts and a neocloud wobble
editions.notification: Amazon's AWS grew 39% but free cash flow turned deeply negative. Here is why AI spending is squeezing Big Tech.
editions.intro:
Amazon dominated the period. Its third-quarter results showed Amazon Web Services growing 39% to $46bn, with a backlog of $578bn, but revenue and earnings per share came in slightly below forecasts and shares fell as much as 7% in extended trading. Free cash flow over the past year slipped to minus $42.4bn, largely from AI capital spending. Chief executive Andy Jassy said AWS should grow more than 40% in 2027 and 2028 and that Amazon will spend meaningfully more on AI next year.

The cash squeeze is a wider theme. A Reuters analysis of LSEG data finds that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned the smallest share of their cash to shareholders in at least 15 years, with buybacks down 83%. Their combined capital spending of $556.9bn exceeded operating cash flow, leaving a free cash flow deficit of $14bn. Meanwhile Microsoft is offering voluntary severance to about 60,000 staff while protecting AI-critical teams, and its AI infrastructure budget is about $170bn for 2026.

Doubts about the AI build-out are growing. Shares in neocloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have fallen by about a quarter in a month, and Nvidia quietly lowered published bandwidth targets for its Vera Rubin hardware. Reports also say OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10bn. Against that backdrop, Oracle shares rose about 14% during its AI World conference, though they remain well below their late 2025 high.

top_stories.title: AWS grows 39% but Amazon's cash burn deepens
top_stories.summary: Amazon posted record operating margins and a 39% jump in AWS revenue, but results were slightly below forecasts and shares fell sharply after hours. Free cash flow of minus $42.4bn shows how heavily AI spending is weighing on the business, and Jassy signalled more investment in 2027.

top_stories.title: Big Tech buybacks fall 83% as AI spending outruns cash
top_stories.summary: Five hyperscalers returned the smallest share of cash to shareholders in at least 15 years. Their capex exceeded operating cash flow, with the gap funded by reserves, borrowing and share sales, despite more than $3tn in AI commitments.

top_stories.title: Microsoft offers voluntary severance to a quarter of staff
top_stories.summary: Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, excluding data centres, sales, cybersecurity and quantum teams. It is the second such programme this year and comes as it keeps AI infrastructure spending near $170bn.

top_stories.title: Neocloud shares slump as bubble fears grow
top_stories.summary: CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital have lost about a quarter of their value in a month, weighed by heavy debt and rising borrowing costs. A Microsoft deal cancellation and lower spending forecasts have added to the unease.

top_stories.title: Nvidia quietly trims Vera Rubin bandwidth specs
top_stories.summary: Nvidia reduced published memory and interconnect bandwidth for Vera Rubin hardware without a press release. Analysts read it as a fallback after memory suppliers struggled to hit target speeds, which could help AMD's rival parts look better on paper.

top_stories.title: OpenAI reportedly cuts fundraising target by $10bn
top_stories.summary: According to the Financial Times, OpenAI is now seeking about $20bn at a valuation near $1.25tn, a reduction that is framed as tempering ambitions amid sector anxiety. Details are limited in the available summary.

top_stories.title: Apple reportedly plans iPhone AI features in China via Alibaba
top_stories.summary: The South China Morning Post reports Apple intends to launch AI features on iPhones in China in December through an Alibaba partnership. Scope, regulatory approval and terms are unclear, and Apple has not commented in the available text.

rumour_watch.note: Credible-sounding plan from a major outlet, but based on a short summary with no Apple confirmation; regulatory approval in China is the key hurdle.

in_brief.line: Investors are reportedly trimming growth stock exposure over worries about US economic reliance on AI spending, with money moving into bonds.
Binance says about 90% of the $6.3bn stolen in a record hack has been replaced, with withdrawals set to reopen on 1 November.
The FDA has proposed withdrawing Amgen's Tavneos over liver injury and data manipulation claims; a US court hearing on a settlement was due 29 October.
French lawmakers approved an amendment for a traffic-based levy on content delivery, pending further budget votes in early November.
GM will pay $220m to 35 US states and DC to settle claims it sold driver data to brokers and insurers.
OpenAI will use Daybreak Blue cybersecurity session data for training from 29 November, prompting backlash and a promised opt-out.
Anthropic is adding a text watermark to several Claude models, though a parameter change can avoid it on two older models.

Finance.title: Midterm blue wave sends US tech stocks into correction
Finance.notification: Wall Street's worst day since April 2025 as the Nasdaq slides into correction after the midterms
Finance.summary:
US stocks had their worst session since April 2025 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The Nasdaq fell 5.52% into correction territory, the S&P 500 dropped 4.36% and the Dow lost 3.44%. Investors fear that a Democratic-led Congress and newly elected state officials will curb data centre and AI expansion, and chipmakers and data-centre names took the heaviest losses.

The sell-off spread quickly. Asian chip stocks were hit hard, with Seoul's Kospi triggering a circuit breaker and Japan's Nikkei and Taiwan's TAIEX also falling sharply. In Britain, the Bank of England is widely expected to raise its base rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since August 2023, as inflation climbed to 3.5%. In Europe, BMW's profit fell as China weakened, and the eurozone inflation rate reached 4%.

Some analysts argue the sell-off may be overdone, noting that the S&P 500 has historically risen in the year after midterm votes. Gridlock in Washington could limit sweeping policy changes, though investors also weigh the risk of shutdowns and debt-ceiling fights.

highlights.text: Kospi fell below 5,000 and triggered a circuit breaker; Samsung and SK Hynix led losses as AI worries hit chip stocks.

highlights.label: Oil
highlights.text: Brent fell sharply on Mideast peace hopes, with Trump saying he had no immediate plans to strike Iran.

highlights.text: Voters approved nearly every datacentre moratorium or restriction on the ballot across at least 40 jurisdictions.

points.text: Philadelphia chip index slid 12.3%, its worst day since March 2020, after weak-seeming results from Qualcomm and Arm.

Brent fell more than 8% overnight, its steepest one-day drop since May, and Indian shares rebounded.
French unions called a nationwide strike while budget talks remain deadlocked, extending more than a month of protests.

World.title: Democrats win Congress; markets slide on AI and data-centre fears
World.notification: Democrats take Congress as US midterms shake markets. Tech stocks fall sharply on data-centre regulation fears.
World.summary:
Democrats have won control of Congress in the 3 November US midterms, taking the Senate and moving to a House majority. Trump says he will accept the result and work with Democrats, though he has also threatened vetoes. The result gives Democrats power to check his agenda and open investigations for the remaining two years of his term.

The political shock has spilled into markets. Analysts linked a sharp sell-off in US tech stocks, with the Nasdaq reportedly down about 5.5%, to expectations of tighter rules on AI data centres, particularly in Texas, where the new governor says expansion must pause. Oil fell for a fourth session on lower Iran-war escalation risk, and Asian markets rallied on the view that the result and Iran diplomacy could ease pressure.

Beyond Washington, the Bank of England raised rates for the first time since 2023, France faces a nationwide strike, and Spain's transport minister is resigning after a deadly train crash. Hong Kong's Joshua Wong received a 10-year sentence under the national security law.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrats won the Senate and are projected to win the House, giving them a check on Trump. Trump says he will work with them but may veto bills.

highlights.label: US markets
highlights.text: Nasdaq reportedly fell about 5.5% as investors priced in tighter AI data-centre rules. Nvidia and chip stocks led the losses.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: The Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and warned further rises are becoming more likely. Mortgage holders and savers are affected.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Hundreds of thousands joined French strikes and marches over living costs. Police made at least 448 arrests and the government faces a divided parliament.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion under the national security law. Rights groups condemned the ruling as cruel and unjust.

points.text: Trump says a Russia-Ukraine deal is near after meeting Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev; Abu Dhabi talks are planned for 10 and 11 November.
Spain's transport minister will resign after two deadly train crashes in under a year, the latest reported to have killed 69 people.
Oil fell for a fourth straight session as the risk of escalation in the Iran war appeared to ease.
Indian stocks surged near three-month highs, with the Sensex up about 1,400 points, as Brent slid to around $94.
The UK agreed to time-bound talks on slavery; PM Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology but ruled out reparations.
Incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa says data-centre expansion must stop until laws protect residents, weighing on Nvidia and Oracle.

Tech.title: Tech shares slump as midterms fuel AI slowdown fears
Tech.notification: Global tech stocks plunge after US midterms raise fears of tighter rules on AI data centres
Tech.summary:
Tech shares have fallen sharply across the US, Europe and Asia after Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Campaigns focused on slowing data centre and AI growth, and investors have reacted by selling chipmakers and other AI-linked stocks. The Nasdaq Composite closed down more than 5.5% on Thursday, entering correction territory, while Japan's Nikkei fell 6.3% and South Korea's Kospi triggered a circuit breaker after falling more than 8%.

The sell-off has been driven by expectations of a national moratorium on data centres and tougher scrutiny of AI firms, which Democrats have promised. Nvidia, AMD, Micron and Infineon fell sharply, and Tesla and SpaceX also dropped. President Trump blamed his opponents for the fall. Other stories this week point to the same pressure: a Democratic-led Congress, local ballot measures restricting data centres, and OpenAI and Amazon dropping NDAs for data centre projects.

Beyond the markets, the political backlash is spreading. Elon Musk's spending on Republican candidates failed to deliver wins, and some tech figures are now looking to space as an alternative home for data centres. Meanwhile, AMD posted a record quarter driven by data centre demand, showing that the AI boom and the political backlash are pulling in opposite directions.

highlights.text: The Nasdaq fell about 5.5% on Thursday, its worst day in 18 months, with Nvidia down 9.2% and the VIX up 61%.

Fashion.title: Kering's creative exodus deepens as Balenciaga's Piccioli exits
Fashion.notification: Balenciaga's creative director is out after less than two years, the third Kering exit in weeks.
Fashion.summary:
Kering's creative upheaval deepened this week as Pierpaolo Piccioli left Balenciaga after less than two years in the role. Kering says a successor will be named shortly. Reports put Balenciaga's 2025 sales at €1.47 billion, down from €1.65 billion, and his two shows drew mixed reviews. He follows Seán McGirr at McQueen and Anthony Vaccarello at Saint Laurent out of the group, leaving Kering's biggest houses without creative directors.

The backdrop is a group under pressure. Kering's third-quarter revenue was flat at 3.35 billion euros, with Gucci sales down 6% at constant exchange rates, worse than expected. Chief executive Luca de Meo is restructuring the group, and the stock fell on the day.

Elsewhere, the business of luxury showed mixed signs. Ralph Lauren beat forecasts and raised its outlook, yet a separate report says its revenue forecast disappointed. Burberry's chief executive is pushing a turnaround built on British heritage, and Swaine opened in Paris. Chinese wealth is flowing into jewellery in Hong Kong, a bright spot for the sector.
